metadata.note: The lesson names no assigned reading. Reading questions rest on documents the lesson cites and quotes (Nakamoto, Douceur, Decker and Wattenhofer, the Bitcoin.org developer guides, Payment Processing, the Arbitrum glossary), and each states a fact that is on a visible slide. Only the visible slides before the first content-hidden block count; the hidden slides get no questions. Coverage: one question for each visible check, worked, practice, answers and review slide and the proof-of-work slide, plus the trust, consensus, ledger, confirmation and proof-of-stake slides. The Raft and PBFT (crash and Byzantine fault tolerance) questions of the earlier bank moved to the 01-PC bank, and the n = 3t + 1 questions were dropped.

questions.question_stem: An agent's draft says: "The chain is immutable, so this payment can never be undone." The payment is two minutes old, in Bitcoin's newest block. Which rewrite is accurate?
questions.correct_answer: Say the record is tamper-evident, give its confirmation count and the time read, and say the newest blocks can still be replaced.
incorrect_answers: Keep "immutable", and add that the payment is final, because Bitcoin declares a payment final once it is in any block.
Say the record is tamper-evident, and add that the payment is final, because hash-chaining stops anyone replacing new blocks.
Replace "immutable" with "trustless", because no single party owns the record, so nothing on it can ever be undone later.
questions.explanation: Hashes and copies make an edit to old entries show, so the record is tamper-evident, but the newest blocks can still be replaced while two valid versions compete. Bitcoin never declares a payment final, so the sentence gives the count and the time read.
questions.lesson_block: Check: fix "immutable, so the record is certain"
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-CM-consensus_in_distributed_systems_and_blockchains_intro.qmd: Check: fix "immutable, so the record is certain"

questions.question_stem: An attacker runs a thousand Bitcoin nodes from one rented server, each with its own identity, hoping to outvote the network. Why does the attacker's history not win?
questions.correct_answer: Nodes follow the chain with the most work, and a thousand nodes on one server add no mining power.
incorrect_answers: Each node's vote is weighted by the ETH locked up behind it, and the attacker's nodes hold none of that.
Nodes follow the history most nodes hold, and a thousand nodes are still too few to outnumber the network.
Nodes count identities, but the network drops duplicate identities that come from one server address.
questions.explanation: Bitcoin does not count nodes; it follows the chain with the most work. Extra identities add no work, so the attacker's history has no more work than before. What would work is most of the mining power, which costs real hardware and electricity.
questions.lesson_block: Check: can a thousand fake nodes outvote?
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-CM-consensus_in_distributed_systems_and_blockchains_intro.qmd: Check: can a thousand fake nodes outvote?

questions.question_stem: Two transfers are each two minutes old: one on Tron, whose explorer shows its block as solidified, and one on Bitcoin. What can the analyst state?
questions.correct_answer: Tron as settled, since a solidified block no longer rolls back; Bitcoin only with its confirmation count and time read.
incorrect_answers: Both as settled, because two minutes have passed on each chain and both chains treat that age as final, so no recheck.
Neither as settled, because no chain finalizes a transfer within two minutes, so even a solidified block can still roll back.
Bitcoin as settled, because the transfer is in a block, and Tron only after six confirmations have passed on it.
questions.explanation: The answer depends on each chain's rule, not the clock. Tron's documentation says a solidified block does not roll back. On Bitcoin, two minutes is likely no more than one confirmation, so the analyst gives the count and the time read, and checks again.
questions.lesson_block: Check: two transfers, two minutes old. Settled?
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-CM-consensus_in_distributed_systems_and_blockchains_intro.qmd: Check: two transfers, two minutes old. Settled?

questions.question_stem: An agent asks whether miners were blocking a suspect's Bitcoin transfer that has sat unconfirmed for six hours. You looked on one public explorer. Which wording is right?
questions.correct_answer: Unconfirmed at the time read, on one explorer's mempool view; a low fee, miners leaving it out or a relay fault is not ruled out.
incorrect_answers: Censored by the miners, because six hours is far longer than the wait that Bitcoin's usual six confirmations allow for, so it was blocked.
Rejected by the network, because a transaction not mined within an hour has failed, so it is no longer pending at all.
Unconfirmed on every node, because all full nodes share one global mempool, and the explorer simply displays that list.
questions.explanation: There is no single mempool: each full node keeps its own, so an explorer shows one view. A low fee, miners leaving the transaction out on purpose and a relay problem all leave the same symptom, so the analyst reports what was seen and lists what cannot be ruled out.
questions.lesson_block: Check: a transfer is stuck. What do you write?
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-CM-consensus_in_distributed_systems_and_blockchains_intro.qmd: Check: a transfer is stuck. What do you write?

questions.question_stem: Block 277,321 is the latest when you read Alice's payment, which sits in block 277,316. How many confirmations does it have, and what do you write?
questions.correct_answer: Six (277,321 minus 277,316 plus 1): write six confirmations at the time read, though Bitcoin never declares the payment final.
incorrect_answers: Five (277,321 minus 277,316): write five confirmations, not counting the block the payment sits in, at the time read.
Six (277,321 minus 277,316 plus 1): write that the payment is final, because six is Bitcoin's own rule for finality.
Five (277,321 minus 277,316): write that the payment is final, because five is the count Bitcoin treats as fully settled.
questions.explanation: A transaction's confirmations count its own block and every block on top, so the count is latest height minus the payment's height plus one: six. Bitcoin never declares a payment final, and six is only the usual wait for high-value payments. The sentence carries the time read, because the count keeps rising.
questions.lesson_block: Worked: count Alice's confirmations
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-CM-consensus_in_distributed_systems_and_blockchains_intro.qmd: Worked: count Alice's confirmations

questions.question_stem: A 2 BTC payment sits in Bitcoin block 900,000, and block 900,001 is the latest when you look. What do you tell the agent?
questions.correct_answer: Two confirmations at the time read, short of the usual six; Bitcoin never declares it final, so check again before reporting.
incorrect_answers: One confirmation at the time read, because only the block on top of the payment's own block counts toward its total, not that block.
Final, because a second block now sits on the payment's block, and a second block is enough to make it final for good.
Two confirmations, which is enough to state it as fact, since two blocks make a payment final on every chain at once.
questions.explanation: The count is 900,001 minus 900,000 plus 1, which is two. Two is short of the usual six, and Bitcoin never calls a payment final, so the sentence gives the count and the time read, and the analyst checks again before reporting it.
questions.lesson_block: Practice: how final are three transfers?
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-CM-consensus_in_distributed_systems_and_blockchains_intro.qmd: Practice: how final are three transfers?

questions.question_stem: An Arbitrum One transfer is a minute old. The sequencer has confirmed it, but its batch has not been posted to Ethereum. What do you write?
questions.correct_answer: Confirmed by the sequencer, a semi-trusted promise; not final on Ethereum until its batch is final there.
incorrect_answers: Final on Arbitrum, because the sequencer's confirmation is a vote by validators that cannot be reversed.
Final once the 6.4-day challenge period ends, as that wait applies to every transfer, not just withdrawals.
Confirmed, and final as soon as Ethereum's next block is added, whether the batch is posted or not.
questions.explanation: Arbitrum's soft confirmation is the sequencer's promise. Hard finality comes only when the transfer's batch is posted to Ethereum and final there, so the sentence says confirmed by the sequencer, not yet final. The 6.4-day wait applies to withdrawals to Ethereum.
questions.lesson_block: Answers: three transfers, and the word for each
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-CM-consensus_in_distributed_systems_and_blockchains_intro.qmd: Answers: three transfers, and the word for each

questions.question_stem: Before reading a chain, what should an analyst expect it to tell them about a transfer?
questions.correct_answer: What was recorded, when, and how final it is; who did it is a separate judgment, and why it stalled is not on the chain.
incorrect_answers: What was recorded, when, and how final it is, plus who controls the addresses, because a final record names its owner.
What was recorded and who did it, with a confidence word; whether it is final is left to the agent to decide later.
What was recorded and why a delayed transfer never confirmed, since a miner's reason is part of the block record.
questions.explanation: The chain tells the analyst what was recorded, when, and how final it is. Attribution is a judgment that needs its own evidence and a confidence word, and a delay may mean congestion, censorship or a relay problem, so the analyst names the explanations that cannot be ruled out.
questions.lesson_block: Review: "final" depends on the chain
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-CM-consensus_in_distributed_systems_and_blockchains_intro.qmd: Review: "final" depends on the chain

questions.question_stem: What does a Bitcoin miner do to win the right to add a block?
questions.correct_answer: Changes the nonce and hashes the block's header again and again until the hash falls below the target, at real cost.
incorrect_answers: Hashes each waiting transaction once and wins if its transactions' summary is the lowest hash that any miner submits.
Collects votes from other miners, each vote weighted by the computing work behind it, until two-thirds of that work agrees.
Guesses an account nonce for its address until the hash of the whole block falls below the target, at little cost.
questions.explanation: The miner hashes the block's header: the previous block's hash, a summary of its transactions, the time and a nonce. No one can predict which nonce works, so the only way is to guess and check, and every guess costs computing time and electricity.
questions.lesson_block: Proof of work is guessing until a hash is low
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-CM-consensus_in_distributed_systems_and_blockchains_intro.qmd: Proof of work is guessing until a hash is low

questions.question_stem: Which statement says correctly where the trust sits on Bitcoin and on Tron?
questions.correct_answer: Bitcoin: most of the mining power not attacking together. Tron: its 27 elected Super Representatives, who make blocks.
incorrect_answers: Bitcoin: on the 27 elected Super Representatives. Tron: on most of the mining power never attacking together.
Neither: both chains are trustless, because cryptography replaces every party the system might otherwise need.
Bitcoin: on the sequencer that puts its transactions in order. Tron: on the exchange that holds users' coins for its users.
questions.explanation: A blockchain is not trustless: the trust moves to cryptography, the consensus rules and an assumption about the participants. On Bitcoin it sits on most of the mining power not attacking together; on Tron, on 27 elected Super Representatives; on Arbitrum, on its sequencer.
questions.lesson_block: "Trustless" is wrong: the trust just moves
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-CM-consensus_in_distributed_systems_and_blockchains_intro.qmd: "Trustless" is wrong: the trust just moves

questions.question_stem: Alice signs two payments spending the same coins, one to Carol and one to Dave, and different nodes see a different one first. What does consensus promise?
questions.correct_answer: Honest nodes accept one history and never disagree on a decided entry, and the ledger keeps growing despite faults.
incorrect_answers: Both payments are kept, because each is valid on its own, and the signatures decide which of them is paid first.
Each node keeps the payment it saw first, so different copies may keep different payments until the nodes compare them.
The hash links choose the earlier payment, because a hash shows which of two valid transactions was signed first.
questions.explanation: Signatures and hashes show that each transaction is well formed, but they cannot choose between two that conflict. Consensus makes honest nodes accept the same history. Safety means honest nodes never disagree about a decision; liveness means the ledger keeps growing despite faults.
questions.lesson_block: Consensus decides which history we all accept
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-CM-consensus_in_distributed_systems_and_blockchains_intro.qmd: Consensus decides which history we all accept

questions.question_stem: Three agencies keep one incident log and none is in charge. Which of a ledger's three additions answers who decides the order of entries?
questions.correct_answer: Consensus: a rule all the parties agree in advance for what is added next and in what order.
incorrect_answers: Replication: every agency holds a full copy, so the agency holding the most entries sets the order.
Hash-linking: each block holds the previous block's hash, so the hashes sort the entries by time.
The append-only log: entries are added only at the end, so the first agency to write sets the order.
questions.explanation: A ledger is a log kept by many parties with three additions. Replication answers who holds the record, hash-linking answers how an edit shows, and consensus answers who decides the order of what is added next.
questions.lesson_block: A ledger is a shared log no one can quietly edit
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-CM-consensus_in_distributed_systems_and_blockchains_intro.qmd: A ledger is a shared log no one can quietly edit

questions.question_stem: An attacker with less than half of Bitcoin's mining power mines a private chain that leaves out Alice's payment. What happens as blocks build on the payment?
questions.correct_answer: The attacker's chance of catching up falls exponentially with each block it is behind, but never reaches zero.
incorrect_answers: The attacker's chance falls to zero after six blocks, which is the point at which Bitcoin declares a payment final.
The attacker's chance stays the same, because only the work of its private chain decides which chain wins.
The attacker's chance rises with each block, because it can forge the signatures and rewrite the recent blocks.
questions.explanation: With less than half the mining power, an attacker's chance of catching up falls exponentially with each block behind but never reaches zero, which is why confirmations lower the risk and never end it. Even a majority attacker can rewrite recent blocks but cannot forge a signature.
questions.lesson_block: Each confirmation makes reversal harder
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-CM-consensus_in_distributed_systems_and_blockchains_intro.qmd: Each confirmation makes reversal harder

questions.question_stem: On Ethereum an explorer shows a block as finalized. What does that mean, and what would reversing it cost?
questions.correct_answer: Validators holding two-thirds of staked ETH voted for its checkpoint; reversing it costs at least a third of all stake.
incorrect_answers: Its 12-second slot has passed, so reversing it would cost only the one proposer that staked a 32 ETH deposit, nothing more.
Six blocks now sit on it, so reversing it would take most of the network's computing power for about an hour.
The sequencer has confirmed it, so reversing it would cost nothing until its batch is posted to Ethereum, which is slow.
questions.explanation: Ethereum's finality is a protocol state: when votes from at least two-thirds of all staked ETH cover a pair of checkpoints, the older one is finalized with every block before it. Reversing it would cost the attackers at least a third of all staked ETH, because the rules destroy the stake of validators who vote for two conflicting histories.
questions.lesson_block: Proof of stake finalizes by a two-thirds vote
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-CM-consensus_in_distributed_systems_and_blockchains_intro.qmd: Proof of stake finalizes by a two-thirds vote

questions.question_stem: As Nakamoto's white paper describes it, how do nodes choose among competing chains, and why does that make an old block costly to rewrite?
questions.correct_answer: They follow the chain with the greatest total work, so a rewrite must redo that block's work and the work of every block after it.
incorrect_answers: They follow the chain held by the most nodes, so a rewrite needs most of the whole network to switch to the new copy.
They follow the chain with the most transactions, so a rewrite must refill the old block with more transactions than before.
They follow the chain whose newest block has the lowest hash, so a rewrite needs only one lucky guess at that block now.
questions.explanation: Nodes follow the chain with the greatest total work. To rewrite an old block an attacker must redo its work and the work of every later block, faster than the honest miners add new ones.
questions.lesson_block: Proof of work is guessing until a hash is low
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-CM-consensus_in_distributed_systems_and_blockchains_intro.qmd: Proof of work is guessing until a hash is low
questions.specific_source_reading: Nakamoto, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System: nodes follow the chain with the greatest total work; each guess spends CPU time and electricity, as the slide states it

questions.question_stem: Douceur's Sybil attack is one party creating many identities. Why do open chains make influence cost something instead of counting identities?
questions.correct_answer: Anyone can create a thousand identities for almost nothing, so a head count is easy to win; work or stake cannot be faked.
incorrect_answers: Counting identities is too slow for strangers, so work or stake is used to speed up how fast each vote is tallied.
Strangers cannot be trusted to vote honestly, so open chains count only the votes of members who were named in advance.
Identities are checked against a register by the network, but the checks are slow, so cost replaces the register.
questions.explanation: On an open chain anyone can create identities, so a head count could be outvoted by a crowd of fake ones. Making influence cost computing work or locked-up stake means a thousand identities buy nothing. Ledgers with known members can count votes instead.
questions.lesson_block: Open chains buy openness with slower finality
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-CM-consensus_in_distributed_systems_and_blockchains_intro.qmd: Open chains buy openness with slower finality
questions.specific_source_reading: Douceur, The Sybil Attack: one party can present many identities; open chains therefore weigh influence by work or stake, as the slide states it

questions.question_stem: Bitcoin's developer guide calls the usual wait of six confirmations "somewhat arbitrary". What does that mean for how an analyst writes a report?
questions.correct_answer: Six is a convention, not a rule, so the analyst states the count relied on and the time read, never calling it final.
incorrect_answers: Six is a protocol limit, so the analyst may write final once a payment reaches six, whatever its size or the time.
Six is a fixed wait that applies only to small payments, so a high-value payment needs a larger number set by the network.
Six is a rule that Ethereum copied from Bitcoin, so the analyst can use six for any chain's payment, whatever its rule.
questions.explanation: Bitcoin never declares a payment final; six confirmations, about an hour, is the usual wait for high-value payments, and the developer guide itself calls the number somewhat arbitrary. The analyst names the count and the time read so the agent can judge it.
questions.lesson_block: Each confirmation makes reversal harder
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-CM-consensus_in_distributed_systems_and_blockchains_intro.qmd: Each confirmation makes reversal harder
questions.specific_source_reading: Bitcoin.org developer guide and Bitcoin Project, Payment Processing: six confirmations is the usual wait for high-value payments; the guide calls the number somewhat arbitrary, as the slide states it

questions.question_stem: Bitcoin's developer guide says a transaction paying the minimum fee "should be prepared to wait a long time". Why?
questions.correct_answer: Miners pick mostly by fee per byte, so a minimum-fee transaction is passed over for better-paying ones.
incorrect_answers: Nodes drop minimum-fee transactions from relay, so the sender must rebroadcast before any miner can see it.
Miners must take transactions in the order their node first received them, and minimum-fee ones arrive last.
It must wait for the next target adjustment, every 2,016 blocks, before any miner may include it at all.
questions.explanation: Each full node keeps its own mempool, and miners pick transactions mostly by fee per byte. A minimum-fee transaction can wait a long time for a quiet block, so a stuck transfer may mean a low fee, not censorship.
questions.lesson_block: Delay may mean congestion, not censorship
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-CM-consensus_in_distributed_systems_and_blockchains_intro.qmd: Delay may mean congestion, not censorship
questions.specific_source_reading: Bitcoin.org developer guide, Transactions and P2P Network: miners choose mostly by fee per byte; a minimum-fee transaction should be prepared to wait a long time, as the slide states it

questions.question_stem: Two Bitcoin miners find valid blocks at nearly the same time, and the next block extends one of them. What happens to the transactions in the other block?
questions.correct_answer: That block becomes stale and its transactions go back into the mempool to wait for a later block.
incorrect_answers: Those transactions are cancelled, and each sender must sign them again before any miner can include them.
Those transactions stay in the stale block, which nodes keep as a second record of the same history.
Those transactions are confirmed in both blocks, so each of them has two confirmations at the same time.
questions.explanation: Network delay makes nodes differ on which block came first. Nodes follow the chain with the most work, so when the next block extends one side the other becomes stale. Its transactions return to the mempool and can be mined again, with no attacker involved.
questions.lesson_block: A stale block is routine, not an attack
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-CM-consensus_in_distributed_systems_and_blockchains_intro.qmd: A stale block is routine, not an attack
questions.specific_source_reading: Decker and Wattenhofer, Information Propagation in the Bitcoin Network, and Bitcoin.org P2P Network guide: delay lets two blocks compete; a stale block's transactions return to the mempool, as the slide states it

questions.question_stem: Per the Arbitrum glossary, when is an Arbitrum One transfer hard-final, and how long does a withdrawal to Ethereum wait?
questions.correct_answer: Once its batch is posted to Ethereum and final there; a withdrawal waits a 6.4-day challenge period.
incorrect_answers: Once the sequencer confirms it; a withdrawal waits 6.4 minutes, which is about one Ethereum epoch of time.
Once six Ethereum blocks sit on its batch; a withdrawal waits about an hour for those six blocks to settle.
Once 19 of 27 elected producers have built on it; a withdrawal waits 6.4 days for that vote to pass there.
questions.explanation: Arbitrum's soft finality is the sequencer's promise. Hard finality comes when the batch is posted to Ethereum and final there, and a withdrawal to Ethereum also waits out a 6.4-day challenge period. The figures carry their date (23 Oct 2026) because upgrades change them.
questions.lesson_block: Each chain puts a different number on "final"
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-CM-consensus_in_distributed_systems_and_blockchains_intro.qmd: Each chain puts a different number on "final"
questions.specific_source_reading: Arbitrum glossary (Offchain Labs): soft finality is the sequencer's promise, hard finality is the batch final on Ethereum, withdrawals wait a 6.4-day challenge period [23 Oct 2026], as the slide states it
